newsitem.title: UK: Dollar stabilises in Europe amid calls for calm.
newsitem.headline: Dollar stabilises in Europe amid calls for calm.

text.p: Calls from Japanese officials for calmer markets on Tuesday helped stabilise the dollar in Europe following recent wild gyrations, traders said.

At midsession, the U.S. unit was slightly higher on the yen and slightly weaker on the mark compared with Monday but its trading ranges were narrower than of late. Dealers reported nervy pricing, however, and the dollar was off early highs.

"This has been such a choppy, rumour-driven market in recent days that the market seems to have stalled itself until a more concrete fix on events feeds through," said Julian Jessop, international economist at Nikko Europe.
Earlier today, Japan's finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee he expects foreign exchange markets to settle down soon at an appropriate level.
Bank of Japan director Yutaka Yamaguchi said it was important for foreign exchange rates to stabilise at levels reflecting economic fundamentals.

Last week, Japanese ministry of finance officials had precipitated the biggest one-week dollar/yen decline since 1989 by warning currency markets about possible intervention to prevent further yen weakness. This combined with growing talk of a Japanese interest rate rise to send the dollar into tailspin.
At 1050 GMT, the dollar was trading at 118.90/00 yen compared with 118.67/77 late Monday but off its early high at 119.65. Against the mark, it was at 1.6980/85 compared with 1.7010/20 late Monday.

"A raft of comments from Japanese officials helped stabilise the situation and I think they were genuinely taken aback by the sheer speed of the dollar's fall since last week," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America.
Traders dismissed a series of rumours and market chat ranging from concern Bank of Japan was poised to sell dollars to extend its fall to talk of a Japanese rate rise as soon as this week.
Toyota Motor Corp chairman Shoichiro Toyoda said earlier that a dollar range of 110-to-120 yen was appropriate.

Analysts said any dollar recovery would also be limited before the release at 1230 GMT of the April U.S. retail sales report. Sales in April are expected to be soft and analysts polled by Reuters expect a 0.3 percent drop during the month.

A weak sales report would further dampen speculation the Federal Reserve will move to lift interest rates again next week. The scaling back of these expectations was partly responsible for the dollar's sharp retreat last week.
Elsewhere, sterling rallied from early lows.

The pound received a boost from the Bank of England's (BOE) quarterly inflation report, now seen as key for the UK interest rate outlook since the bank was given operational independence by the new Labour government last week.

The central bank report said the strength of sterling would see the underlying UK inflation falling well below the 2.5 percent government target this year but that further interest rate rises were needed to maintain that two years out.
The BOE said that sterling strength is hurting output and exports less than it had thought in February and it was rapid growth in the service sector which was inflationary.
"The surprise is that they (the BOE) are still calling for another tightening of policy before see the effects of the last one," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

The Australian dollar retreated from session highs, meantime, after the Australian government's budget forecasts for the 1997/1998 fiscal year were more modest than expectations. Analyst said a failure to make tough spending cuts worried the bond markets despite the forecast of an underlying budget surplus the following year.
The local dollar had risen prior to the announcment.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
